title: Stop Blundering
reviewNotes: Reviewed montage and narration: this is a middlegame blunder-check lesson with many pieces, covering Bd3/Qxd4, a pawn fork and an overloaded queen. It is not an endgame reconstruction candidate; preserve the original clip in the searchable full-channel archive.

I had a look at a few of your games and I want to help you blunder less. This is day seven of reviewing one of my followers games every single day until I reach 100,000 followers. If you want to be next, all you have to do is like this video, follow me, and comment your chess.com username. This is going to be a fork picking up the knight and winning the game for black. The reason why we tend to miss this kind of stuff in our games, whereas we would be able to see them right away in someone else's game, is because usually we tend to be stuck in our own ideas and plans and strategies and trying to find what we are trying to do and we do not pay enough attention to what our opponent is trying to do. At all times, in every game, no matter the position, we need to be aware of the [music] checks that both sides have and the piece that are under attack and that see each other. So, queen takes D5 has to be on your radar. This has to be a move that you have registered and you need to be aware that your queen has to keep track of this pawn for it to not fall. And in particular, as you get closer to the black pieces, especially to the pawns, there's going to be be increasingly high number of moves like these that are available to your opponent. And here you play your third blunder of the game. You go c4. Again, this doesn't do anything to help defend this pawn. This is more of a tactical blunder. You're relying on the fact that the queen is defending the pawn, but this is the only piece defending the pawn. For example, after a move like rook to g8, the queen has to move and you're going to lose your pawn with a check on the next move and with it the bishop is going to fall. Now, in this case your opponent finds an even better resource with rook h to g8 and after you take this pawn they're going to come back here and take the h pawn and you're completely [music] losing. Better safe than sorry, play c3, create a pawn chain, and now the queen is free to move around the board and it will not have to be a babysitter for this pawn. Now, after rook to g8 you can go to h6 and there's no problem. Keep these tips in mind and always make a blunder check before you play your next move and you will gradually see your blunders decreasing.
